item.title: The Iran war tests Senate Democrats' unity as a shutdown deadline approaches
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – Democrats in the Senate are at odds with each other about the wisdom of risking another government shutdown in order to pressure the Trump administration to end the Iran war. Fresh off their sweeping midterm victories, they've barreled straight into high-stakes deliberations about whether to withhold support for a measure to fund the government past a critical Dec. 11 deadline. Key to unlocking their votes, some Democrats say, would be a commitment from their GOP counterparts to include a provision cutting off money for the conflict in the Middle East. "We should not accept a short-term spending deal that continues to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice," four Senate Democrats wrote in a statement last week . "Any short-term package must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran." Others are leery about subjecting the country to a potentially painful shutdown just weeks before the holidays. Vermont Sen. Peter Welch and Nevada Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto told USA TODAY they're against forcing a shutdown to end the war. It would simply cause "a lot of hardship on people," Welch said. "I am absolutely committed to doing everything we can to stop the war," he said. "I'm skeptical a shutdown would help pursue that goal." The divide over how to approach government funding is becoming another fissure in a Democratic Party that swept to commanding majorities in the midterms – but is still contending with high-profile internal battles that threaten to upend the united front it hopes to project against President Donald Trump . The hardball tactics, and disagreements about whether to deploy them, could also be a preview into the dynamics that will shape how Democrats in Congress will approach political strategy heading into the final two years of the Trump administration. But the fight over federal funding is allowing the specter of a shutdown crisis – which can cause intensifying air travel disruptions as TSA workers go without pay – to form over Americans, many of whom are already reeling from last week's nationwide ground stoppage . "As of right now, the Democrats aren't engaging in a conversation at all when it comes to funding the government," Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters this week. "That’s a problem, which again suggests perhaps they are thinking about yet a third government shutdown, which would be a really, really bad outcome for the country." Democrats walking fine line Senate Democrats emerged from their weekly lunch Tuesday saying they had "productive" discussions about the war and government funding. The issue is emerging as a dividing line in the ongoing race for the next Senate majority leader. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the New Yorker who's led Senate Democrats for a decade, has repeatedly said in the same breath that the Iran war must end and a shutdown must be avoided. He hasn't explicitly clarified, however, whether the caucus would be willing to withhold its government funding votes, plunging the country into a preholiday crisis, if its demands over the war aren't met. Because of the Senate's 60-vote threshold, at least some Democrats would need to vote with Republicans in order to avert a funding lapse. Schumer's progressive challenger for majority leader, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, on the other hand, has indicated a shutdown would be worth the pain. "Under our current leadership, we have a situation where they are not willing to use the most important power we have to end the war, which is to defund it," he said at a meeting of Democrats last week in Denver. On the heels of those comments, a telecommunications malfunction affecting air traffic control canceled and delayed many flights across the country last Friday, previewing the same kinds of issues travelers could face in the event of yet another government shutdown. (Funding lapses are known to cause steadily worsening staffing shortages among TSA agents and air traffic controllers as they work temporarily without pay.) Several Senate Democrats have acknowledged they're walking a fine political line. And it's not the first time. In the 119th Congress, Democrats have already been part of two record-breaking government shutdowns that lasted weeks, prompting hundreds of thousands of government employees to go without pay as the consequences trickled down through the economy. Many Americans have come to associate shutdowns with images of hourslong lines at airports. Yet the war in Iran is unpopular across the political spectrum, and the resulting spike in gas prices and other costs was seen as a significant factor driving voter turnout for Democrats. "There's an appreciation that it's really essential that we do not shut the government down," Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said. "But at the same time, we have to find a way to channel the feeling of the American public." Both chambers of Congress already took a largely symbolic vote earlier this year to end the Iran war, and the House of Representatives specifically has passed multiple resolutions to cease hostilities in the region. But "the president's ignored it," Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Virginia, said. In his view, withholding support for government funding has become "the only lever (Democrats) have." At the same time, Senate Republicans have spent the last few days laying the groundwork to fast-track a party-line budget bill that could potentially infuse the Pentagon with hundreds of billions of new dollars. Many of them have continued to balk at the prospect of fully cutting off cash for the war. "That's not gonna happen," Sen. John Kennedy, R-Louisiana, said. "Not in your or mine or our natural lifetimes." Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Is playing hardball on Iran worth a shutdown? Democrats can't decide This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/11/19/government-shutdown-iran-war-pentagon-reconciliation/92831732007/

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin's 'peace declaration' leaves out the wars in Iran and Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on Thursday was the first-ever sit-down for the leaders of the three countries. They started with talk of a shared responsibility for keeping peace as the victors of World War II and as global powers. But post-meeting readouts by the three nations reflected more symbolism than substance. The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. It said they agreed on the need for reforms to the United Nations, on increasing oil supplies and on reducing nuclear risks. The statement did not spell out the type and extent of the U.N. reforms the leaders agreed to. The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, opposing what they called "jurisdiction abuse" by the International Criminal Court, the reports said. Here are key takeaways from the talks, which lasted over an hour. China's Xi presided over the summit of 21st century powers Xi added to China's already burgeoning diplomatic stature merely by hosting the event. He said the talks with Trump and Putin were positive and fruitful, and that the three nations had aligned views on safeguarding world peace, according to China's Xinhua official news agency. They agreed major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously and believe differences should be resolved through negotiation and cooperation, Xinhua reported. "As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," Xi was quoted as saying. "The seeds planted at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit." China's insistence that it has the right to recover the democratically governed island of Taiwan, possibly by force, was not addressed in the leaders' broadly worded agreement. China considers that a domestic issue. China likes to position itself as a different kind of superpower from the U.S. and Russia — one that doesn't get involved in wars and advocates for smaller states, said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. Beijing's priority was steering the meeting away from specifics, she said. "Beijing wanted to be seen as the adult in the room." Trump claims a place in history Trump heralded the leaders' gathering as "really making history" and he suggested to Xi and Putin that together they were shaking things up by ditching the "old school" way adversaries engage. The White House set low expectations for the talks. But Trump framed them Thursday as only the beginning — a chance to get the conversation rolling on solving some of the world's thorniest issues. "A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start," Trump told Putin during a one-on-one meeting prior to their three-way meeting with Xi. The carefully crafted event was a welcome break for Trump after a couple of rotten weeks for his presidency in which his Republican Party was trounced in the midterm elections, widespread tech outages spooked Americans, and Iran escalated attacks on U.S. allies. Trump said Iran was on the agenda. China and Russia carry enormous sway with Tehran and also have been accused by the U.S. of supporting the Islamic Republic. He reiterated Thursday that he and Xi agree Iran needs to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for world energy supplies that has become a chokepoint since the start of the war. They also agree that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon, Trump said. But there were no signs that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict. Putin shares spotlight with Trump and Xi For Putin, the three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit — and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier — offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to signal that he heads a superpower on par with the United States and China. Trump and Putin found common ground in their opposition to the ICC. The Russian leader is wanted by the ICC under an arrest warrant for his alleged war crimes in Ukraine. The U.S. opposes the ICC's arrest warrant against former Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Putin last attended an APEC summit in 2017. His presence as an honored guest and Russia's status as a top global power — at least at the gathering in Shenzhen — mark a diplomatic breakthrough. Just before the summit, Russia sent a pair of nuclear-capable Tu-95 bombers on a visit to Vietnam in a reminder of its nuclear might. And as Putin arrived in China, Russian TV zeroed in on an officer in his retinue who was carrying a briefcase with the codes for Moscow's nuclear forces. Putin addressed Xi as "dear friend" during their talks on Wednesday, and smiled contentedly on Thursday as he shook hands with Trump, who called him "my friend" and boasted about their "great relationship for many years." Speaking at the start of the three-way talks, Putin underscored the global weight of Russia, China and the U.S. The three nations are "united not only by our status as victors in World War II, but, most importantly, by our shared responsibility for maintaining international peace and security," he said. They are also among the founders of the United Nations, Putin noted, adding that "we bear responsibility for preserving and strengthening the system of international law." "Our nations share many common interests regarding the resolution of regional conflicts, including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said. Russia's war in Ukraine featured in Putin's bilateral meetings with Trump and Xi. It wasn't the main topic of the three-way talks, Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. The Kremlin released video of the Chinese leader escorting the Russian president to his car at the end of the talks and the two men shaking hands. "I don't think anyone even expected things to go so well," Putin told Xi as the two men parted ways. ___ Madhani reported from Washington and Leung reported from Hong Kong. item.title: Denmark unanimously approves Greenland security deal with the U.S.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Stine Jacobsen and Tom Little COPENHAGEN, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Denmark's parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future ‌that has rattled transatlantic relations. The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after US President ‌Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people. "This agreement modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defence partnership and ​bolsters the national security of the United States and our allies in NATO," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement posted on X. The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark's foreign ministry tells the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete. It does not need approval from the US Senate. It expands the US military's role in Greenland, including permission to ‌establish a "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while ⁠reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination. The signatories will now start work on a new Greenland law to screen outside investors on security grounds and plans for two new ⁠US military bases, as outlined in the agreement, Denmark’s Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters. "I expect that the US will now also start to be more concrete on the purposes and the arrangement around these two areas," he said. Trump's refusal to rule out ​military or ​economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis ​within NATO in January and months of intensive ‌negotiations. DIFFICULT TIME FOR GREENLANDERS Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the Danish parliament, said Trump's pressure had led to distrust in Greenland towards the US administration. "It's been really difficult for Greenlanders these past two years. It's been seeping into every aspect of our lives," Nathanielsen told Reuters. She hoped the agreement would open a path to dialogue after hurtful rhetoric within the Western alliance. Greenland's parliament ratified the deal this month. Danish lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize ‌the situation in Greenland. Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at ​the University of Copenhagen, said the deal was more likely a ​beginning than an end. "With the treaty in hand, ​the US will be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications ‌and on part of the extraction of strategic ​resources," he said. Other experts say ​the new agreement does not add much US military access to Greenland. The northernmost US base is already in Greenland, which lies on the shortest route from Europe to North America. Trump last month said that "massive oil, ​gas and mineral exploration" was set ‌to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has banned new drilling for crude. ​Denmark has said any resource extraction must respect local law. (Reporting by Stine Jacobsen, editing by Jacob ​Gronholt-Pedersen, Louise Rasmussen, Rod Nickel, Thomas Derpinghaus and Chizu Nomiyama) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/denmark-expected-ratify-trump-deal-050311767.html

item.title: World's top court rules Myanmar acted with 'genocidal intent' against Rohingya
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague delivered its judgement on Thursday about the military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh. ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”. It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court. The ruling marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed. The case was brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, which in 2019 accused Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people. It asked the ICJ to rule that Myanmar breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order it to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished. Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA). Evidence shows Myanmar forces killed 10,000 Rohingya, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict. “The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya ⁠⁠civilians, perpetrated widespread acts ⁠⁠of sexual violence as well as acts of ⁠⁠extreme violence against children and ⁠⁠attacked fleeing Rohingya ⁠⁠as they sought to flee in large numbers to ‌‌Bangladesh,” he added. In specific cases that he referred to, he said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”. The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority. It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added. Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said. The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include: Facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution. ‘Waiting’ years for justice The court established that at least four genocidal acts have been proven, said Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen, reporting from the Hague. They are the mass killing of civilians; the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of people; serious harm inflicted upon the group; and the prevention of birth. The Rohingya have long been treated as second-class citizens, well before 2017, according to the judge, Vaessen said. They were also forced to take part in a birth control programme, she added. “So the judge really saw this as a very strong explanation that … a genocidal act was committed there.” The verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya,” our correspondent said. “They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.” The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide. “The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera. Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”. Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced. More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable. This article originally appeared on Al Jazeera at https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/19/un-top-court-finds-myanmar-killed-10000-rohingya-as-it-rules-on-genocide

item.title: Voyager 1 phones home from a light-day away for the 1st time in space history
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — NASA's Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away , humanity's first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space . Flight controllers received the spacecraft's call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That's how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) at the speed of light. "Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler," NASA's Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement. It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our "Pale Blue Dot" in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun's sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012. NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But that didn't stop the space agency from wishing everyone a "Happy Voyager light-day … day!" via social media the day before. "Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," JPL director Dave Gallagher said in a statement. Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA's longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring. Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won't reach the one-light-day mark until 2035. Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment. No science or engineering data have been received from Voyager 1 since Saturday, according to NASA. However, the carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone. Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped. Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase "Pale Blue Dot" for Voyager 1's farewell glimpse of Earth. NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records — time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them — to last more than 1 billion years. ___ The Associated Press' health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP's standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org . item.title: Costco sees surge in panic buying after a string of tech outages, report says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Consumers are panic-buying at Costco, snapping up generators and other emergency-preparedness items in response to a recent string of technology outages , according to investment firm Mizuho Securities. "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report. Shoppers are "pantry-loading," while 21 of the retailer's 26 "high-ticket generators" were sold out online as of Sunday night, he added. The recent outages, which blocked access to Microsoft apps , snarled flights nationwide and hindered banking activities at various times during the past week, are raising questions among Americans about a larger cybersecurity threat, CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman said on "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday. The companies affected by the outages have said they were due to issues such as routine maintenance or upgrades, while the Federal Aviation Administration blamed its nationwide ground stop last week on a contractor updating its flight system. "All of them have denied that cyberattacks are to blame," Gutman said. "Still, the system failures are fueling online speculation about a larger cyber threat." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that there's "zero evidence" that the recent outages in the U.S. are linked. "The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA . The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said during a news conference in the Philippines. Costco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The close timing of the outages highlights the country's increasing reliance on technology, John D'Arcy, a Temple University professor who researches cybersecurity and information technology failures, told CBS News Philadelphia. "Our systems are so much more complex and so much more interconnected than they ever have been in the past, that when we just have one failure, the effects are much more dramatic," D'Arcy said. The surge in panic buying could lift Costco's sales, Bellinger wrote. He raised his target price for the company's stock to $1,150 from $1,100. Other big-box stores, including Walmart and Sam's Club, could see similar "pantry-loading lifts," he added. item.title: Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official over investigation of her political speech
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., was also one of six Democratic lawmakers targeted by the Trump administration this year over a video they posted to social media. (Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty) WASHINGTON — A Democratic senator repeatedly targeted by the Trump administration for potential prosecution due to her political remarks is firing back at a Trump-appointed Justice Department official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her rhetoric about congressional oversight. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is one of five Democratic members of Congress who have been the subject of letters that the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, has posted on social media. In one of the letters, which have come under scrutiny from legal experts, Reitz suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight potentially acting as a “deterrence message” to people considering joining the Trump administration could amount to a criminal civil rights offense. “I made those statements consistent with my basic right to freedom of speech, a right that every American enjoys under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” Slotkin wrote Wednesday in a letter to Reitz obtained by NBC News. “In addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility.” “The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts,” she wrote. “As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.” Slotkin went on to say that Reitz’s “public threats” violated Justice Department policy, and that his decision to publicly post the letter rather than providing it to her, her attorney or the Senate legal counsel “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.” Reitz, 39, previously worked as chief of staff for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and became U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas over the summer after placing fourth in the Republican primary for state attorney general. Reitz also posted letters on X to Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and Sen. Adam Schiff , D-Calif. He told NBC News this week that he was “not interested in chilling free speech.” Aaron Reitz on Capitol Hill last year. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty ) Slotkin and five other sitting Democratic lawmakers were separately targeted by the Trump administration earlier this year over a video they posted to social media that sought to remind members of the military and intelligence communities that they should not obey unlawful orders. Allies of the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, tried to indict the six Democrats for their speech in that video, but federal grand jurors unanimously rejected the indictment attempt. Slotkin’s attorney, Preet Bharara, had previously written a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche cautioning him against following President Donald Trump’s public instruction to look into Slotkin’s political speech, which he dubbed a “criminal act.” Blanche has conceded that Slotkin’s words alone were “absolutely not a crime” and said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.” Slotkin wrote in her letter that Reitz appeared to be “seeking attention” for himself and the Justice Department, or was “unaware” of basic constitutional rights. “Given all of this, your threats are frivolous and a violation of your ethical duties as an attorney,” she wrote. “I reserve all rights to take appropriate actions in the future as it relates to this sham investigation.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/elissa-slotkin-fires-back-aaron-reitz-investigation-political-speech-rcna610133

item.title: Critics love ‘GTA 6.’ Gamers are not as enthralled.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Grand Theft Auto VI is here at last and gamers around the world can finally play after it launched at midnight globally. So far the game, which takes up a whopping 212GB on your PlayStation5 or Xbox, is receiving rave reviews . GTA 6 is streaming all over Twitch and the memes, clips and hot takes are pouring in. Digital marketing firm Sensor Tower estimates that GTA 6 pre-orders have already topped $1.65 billion in sales. GTA 6 costs $79.99 for PS5 and Xbox , with an "ultimate" version priced at $99.99. Players began pre-loading GTA 6 last week, even though they probably had to clear some space on their consoles. Millions of people are expected to take time off work and school to play GTA 6 . Xbox has a doctor's note from DJ Khaled (aka Dr. Xbox) that may be the excuse you need (but you'll probably want to clear it with your boss either way). item.title: Musk says he feels 'foolish' after spending over $440 million to back Republicans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, expressed buyer’s remorse Wednesday about his massive — and ultimately futile — spending spree to elect Republicans in the midterms. The SpaceX and Tesla founder, who spent over $440 million backing GOP candidates, most of whom lost, acknowledged: “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.” The comments came during The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, where Musk also distanced himself from President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement, maintaining “there are positives and negatives in both parties.” “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that,” Musk said at the event, which he attended virtually from China, as he and other business leaders accompanied President Donald Trump to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. “But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.” Musk, who has experienced an on-again off-again relationship with Trump, was by far the biggest single donor this election cycle, spending at an unprecedented clip to support Republicans. But his efforts failed to make a major impact, as key GOP strongholds such as Texas, where he spent the bulk of his money, and Kansas flipped to Democrats. Despite his midterm spending, Musk sought to clarify during Wednesday’s public interview that he is “not MAGA” — regardless of his ties with the president. Instead, Musk claimed he supported a balance of power between Democrats and Republicans in the government. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” Musk said. These statements conflict with how Musk aligned with Trump in the past, even going as far to label himself as “Dark MAGA” when he campaigned for him just two years ago. In fact, Musk appeared optimistic about working with the newly elected Democratic governor in Texas, where he runs massive SpaceX and Tesla operations. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has criticized the tech billionaire, has also said she is open to a “strong working relationship” with Musk. “The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate,” Musk said. “I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor. And based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/18/musk-says-he-feels-foolish-after-gop-election-spending-spree-01174509
